content: The Copper Family is a group of singers specializing in traditional, unaccompanied English folk songs. They originally hail from Rottingdean, near Brighton in Sussex, England, but the core members of the family now reside in the nearby village of Peacehaven. The Copper Family has maintained a long-standing tradition of singing unaccompanied local folk songs, a practice that has been passed down through multiple generations. In 1904, Lucy Broadwood, one of the founders of the Folk Song Society (later known as the English Folk Dance and Song Society), recognized the unique value of their music. She noted that both the collection of songs and the unaccompanied singing style were less common than often assumed at the time. Broadwood, herself a singer, realized she had discovered something extraordinary when she encountered the Coppers. In 1936, the Copper brothers, John (1879–1952) and Jim (1882–1954), were made honorary members of the Folk Song Society. John, also known as Brasser, was encouraged to document the songs he knew. Later, in 1936, Jim compiled an additional volume of songs. Jim had two children, Joyce (1910–?) and Bob (1915–2004). In 1950, Jim and Bob were invited to perform on an episode of the BBC Radio program Country Magazine. Over the following years, the BBC recorded more of their performances, including a feature titled The Life of James Copper, which aired in September 1951. Bob Copper, along with his brother Ron (1913–1979), continued the family tradition. Together with Jim and John, they performed at prestigious venues such as the Royal Albert Hall. Their music gained wider public attention following the broadcast of a six-part television series, Song Hunter, presented by Alan Lomax, which featured Jim, Bob, and Ron. Bob Copper authored several books about the family and their songs, starting with the highly acclaimed A Song for Every Season in 1971. This book was accompanied by a four-LP set, which has since become a collector's item. The recordings featured Bob and Ron singing alongside Bob’s daughter Jill and son John, thereby introducing another generation into the family tradition. After Ron’s death, Jill’s husband Jon joined the core lineup, and some of Bob’s grandchildren began performing with the group. The six grandchildren—Jill’s children Mark, Andy, and Sean Barratt, and John’s children Ben, Lucy, and Tom Copper—now perform independently as The Young Coppers, continuing the family repertoire. Since the 1950s, various recordings of the Copper Family’s singing have been made, many of which remain available. Notably, the album Come Write Me Down includes two booklets filled with biographical details. Bob Copper passed away in 2004, just days after receiving an MBE (Member of the Order of the British Empire). The current generations of the family continue to sing unaccompanied traditional songs. In 2006, BBC Four aired an hour-long program about the family. They are also involved in The Imagined Village project.
